column2: I'm Lee, and I built Commons on my own: the white paper, the Solana program, the Mac app, and the website.
Most people hold crypto to speculate, not to use it.
New coins go to whoever burns the most electricity, or already holds the most coins.
And developers are funded from a foundation budget that eventually runs out.
C M N is money measured in work. One C M N buys twenty work units: twenty billion metered WebAssembly instructions.
Every day, an on-chain rule reads what compute jobs actually cleared at, and adjusts the money supply to hold that price steady.
C M N can rise with the network's real output, by at most twenty-five percent a year.
New money is first mined by useful work, paid only when independent providers agree on the result.
After that, it flows through banks that users found and can vote out. Banks don't lend. They fund builders, and their operators earn when what they fund is actually used.
So the network's growth keeps funding the people who build on it.
The first users are people who need prices they can plan around: developers selling software, people trading compute, and AI agents paying for computation.
It runs on Solana devnet today: jobs drawn, settled and mined; a Store where apps are bought with C M N and installed only if their hash matches the chain; and banks opened by user vote.
Next: a metered WebAssembly runner, an audit, and mainnet.
Commons. Money that pays for work, and funds the people who build.
